issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s desire to occupy a residential property is a bona fide requirement when it is a genuine, sincere need rather than a mere wish or pretext.
material_facts: The landlord sought possession of a residential property he had built and previously occupied, and it was the only property he owned that was available for his residence.
He was elderly, had declining health and faculties, and wanted to settle in his own home with his wife near his longstanding personal connections.

He admitted negotiating to sell the property to the tenant, but explained that he had considered selling because he thought obtaining possession would be difficult; the negotiations failed and he then decided to live in the property.
The Rent Controller and Appellate Authority found the landlord’s need genuine.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s requirement for his own occupation was bona fide, and the eviction order was justified.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13(3)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the landlord must require the residential building for his own occupation. The requirement must be genuine, honest, conceived in good faith, and reasonable to gratify, rather than a mere desire or pretext. The court assesses the landlord’s need objectively in light of all relevant circumstances. The Court relied on Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander, Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan, Gulabbai v. Nalin Narsi Vohra, and Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta.

rule.if: residential_eviction_proceeding and landlord_seeks_personal_occupation and only_available_owned_residence and (need_supported_by_personal_circumstances or sale_attempt_plausibly_explained)

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking eviction from a residential property on the ground that the landlord requires it for personal occupation.
predicates.landlord_seeks_personal_occupation: The landlord genuinely seeks to occupy the property personally.
predicates.only_available_owned_residence: The property is the only property owned by the landlord that is available for the landlord’s residence.
predicates.need_supported_by_personal_circumstances: The landlord’s circumstances, such as age, health, or personal ties to the home, support the stated need to occupy it.
predicates.sale_attempt_plausibly_explained: The landlord has explained a prior attempt to sell the property in a manner consistent with a genuine later decision to occupy it.

issues.definition: When a residential eviction proceeding involves a landlord who genuinely seeks personal occupation of the only owned residence available to them, supported by personal circumstances or a plausibly explained sale attempt, the requirement is bona fide.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not overturn concurrent factual findings merely because it would draw a different inference from the evidence.
material_facts: The Rent Controller and Appellate Authority both found that the landlord’s need for the property was genuine.
The High Court reversed those findings after drawing a different inference from the landlord’s residence abroad and his earlier negotiations to sell the property.
The Supreme Court found the authorities’ conclusions supported by the evidence and not unreasonable or otherwise unlawful.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the proper scope of revisional review by substituting its different view of the facts, and the concurrent findings were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 confers revisional jurisdiction to examine the legality or propriety of an order or proceeding, not to reappreciate evidence merely because the High Court prefers another factual inference. Intervention may be warranted where a finding is unreasonable, unsupported by the evidence, based on an erroneous legal premise, or lacking objectivity. The Court relied on Ram Dass v. Ishwar Chander, Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Dr. Mahesh Chand Gupta, Mudigonda Chandra Mouli Sastry v. Bhimanepalli Bikshalu, and Lekh Raj v. Muni Lal.

rule.if: rent_control_revision_proceeding and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and high_court_only_prefers_different_inference

predicates.rent_control_revision_proceeding: The case is a revision in a rent-control matter rather than an appeal permitting a fresh determination of the facts.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The first-instance authority and the appellate authority reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The concurrent finding has support in the evidence and is not shown to be unreasonable or legally defective.
predicates.high_court_only_prefers_different_infere: The revisional court departs from the finding because it would draw a different inference from the same evidence.

issues.definition: In a rent-control revision, supported concurrent factual findings are not reopened when the revisional court merely prefers a different inference.

issues.legal_issue: A court may consider subsequent events only when they are promptly and procedurally brought before it, the opposing party has an opportunity to respond, and they materially affect a party’s right to relief.
material_facts: The tenant relied on events during the litigation, including the landlord’s frequent travel to and residence in Canada, his acquisition of Canadian status and citizenship, and his earlier negotiations to sell the property to the tenant.

The landlord had an opportunity to explain the sale negotiations and stated that he had considered selling because he thought it would be difficult to recover possession, but the negotiations failed and he later decided to live in the property.
There was no evidence that the landlord had tried to sell the property to anyone else, before or after those negotiations.
The Supreme Court found that the events did not undermine the established bona fide need and instead reinforced it.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent events did not defeat or weaken the landlord’s bona fide requirement for the property.
issues.legal_principle: A court may take account of subsequent events if they are brought promptly to its attention, presented through procedures that allow the court to consider them and the opposing party to answer them, and have a material bearing on the right to relief. On the facts, the events relied on did not dent the established need; the landlord’s explanation of the negotiations was reasonable and probable. The Court also relied on Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan for the principle that the landlord is the best judge of residential requirements and courts should not dictate how the landlord should live.

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding seeking eviction from a residential property on the ground of the landlord’s personal need.
predicates.subsequent_events_presented_for_consider: Events occurring during the proceeding are brought before the court for consideration and the opposing party has an opportunity to address them.
predicates.landlord_explains_sale_negotiations_cred: The landlord gives a reasonable explanation for prior negotiations to sell the property that is consistent with a later genuine decision to occupy it.
predicates.no_evidence_of_other_sale_attempts: There is no evidence that the landlord attempted to sell the property to other prospective purchasers.

issues.definition: When subsequent events are considered in a residential eviction proceeding, credible explanation of sale negotiations and no evidence of other sale attempts leave the bona fide need intact.
